evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children in India with hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) persisting for 6 months or more: assessment, who to treat under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Program (NVHCP), choice and dosing of tenofovir or entecavir, monitoring, pregnancy and prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and co-infection with HIV or hepatitis C. Built on the NVHCP Technical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hepatitis B (2019).
findings: Definition of chronic infection, use of aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) and fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) cut-offs, elastography thresholds and the whom-to-treat algorithm checked against NVHCP Hepatitis B Technical Guidelines 2019, p. 22.
Adult and paediatric doses of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) and rules for choosing between them checked against Tables 2 and 3, p. 23.
Baseline and follow-up tests, referral to Model Treatment Centres, pregnancy, birth-dose vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin, breastfeeding and children checked against pp. 24–25.
HIV co-infection (tenofovir-based antiretroviral therapy), hepatitis C co-infection and prevention checked against pp. 26–27; renal monitoring and entecavir renal dosing against p. 47.
unverifiedSections: TDF dose interval in reduced creatinine clearance is not given in the NVHCP guideline; the guideline advises entecavir or TAF when eGFR is under 60 mL/min/1.73 m².
Antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy for high viral load is described as unclear in NVHCP 2019; follow current specialist advice.
Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance interval is not stated explicitly in the NVHCP sections used; ultrasound is part of baseline assessment.

The fixed-dose antiretroviral tablet strengths (TDF 300 mg, lamivudine 300 mg, efavirenz 600 mg) are not stated in NVHCP 2019; the National AIDS Control Organisation now favours dolutegravir-based tenofovir regimens — follow the current national ART guideline.
Pegylated interferon is for selected patients at Model Treatment Centres; dosing is not given here.
Drug cautions and contraindications without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.
US labels (DailyMed) were used where Indian sources give no dose; confirm against the Indian product label (CDSCO) and hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined by HBsAg persisting for 6 months or more. India has intermediate endemicity; most infections are acquired at birth or in early childhood, when about 90% of infected newborns become chronic carriers. Many people stay well for years, but some develop cirrhosis, liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Antivirals suppress the virus and prevent progression but rarely cure, so treatment is usually lifelong (NVHCP 2019, p. 18).
keyMechanisms: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists in hepatocytes as covalently closed circular DNA, which drugs do not eradicate.
Immune attack on infected hepatocytes causes inflammation (raised ALT) and progressive fibrosis.
Fibrosis leads to cirrhosis, portal hypertension and decompensation.
Integrated viral DNA and chronic inflammation drive HCC, even without cirrhosis.

symptoms: Usually none; found on screening (antenatal, blood donation, pre-surgery) (NVHCP p. 18)
Jaundice, abdominal swelling or confusion in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Signs of chronic liver disease: palmar erythema, spider naevi
Ascites, pedal oedema in decompensation (NVHCP p. 26)
redFlags: Jaundice, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy or variceal bleeding: decompensated cirrhosis — refer to Model Treatment Centre (NVHCP p. 24)
Flare with jaundice or acute liver failure (NVHCP p. 24)
Stopping tenofovir in HIV co-infection: risk of severe flare (NVHCP p. 27)
Starting chemotherapy or immunosuppression: reactivation risk (NVHCP p. 24)
precipitants: Perinatal transmission from an infected mother (NVHCP p. 18)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Recent exposure within 180 days and high ALT; repeat HBsAg after 6 months to confirm chronicity (NVHCP p. 22).
Anti-HCV positive with detectable HCV RNA.
HBsAg negative; fatty liver on ultrasound with metabolic risk factors.
Alcohol history; AST:ALT ratio often over 2.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: HBsAg positive for 6 months or more.
APRI 2 or more, or FIB-4 3.25 or more, or elastography 12.5 kPa or more.
APRI over 1.5, or FIB-4 over 1.45, or elastography 8.0 kPa or more.

Cirrhosis: treat irrespective of age, ALT, HBeAg or HBV DNA. Non-cirrhotic: treat if HBV DNA over 20,000 IU/mL with persistently raised ALT, or HBV DNA over 2,000 IU/mL with APRI over 1.5, FIB-4 over 1.45 or platelets under 100 ×10⁹/L, particularly if over 30 years.
At least 2 values 4 weeks apart in the last 6 months above the upper limit of normal.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Complete blood count, HBsAg, APRI, liver function tests, abdominal ultrasound and HBV DNA (NVHCP p. 24).
Test for HIV and hepatitis C (NVHCP p. 24).
Assess alcohol use; vaccinate household contacts and sexual partners who are HBsAg negative.

clinicalManagement.title: Decide on treatment
actions: Use the NVHCP whom-to-treat algorithm (NVHCP p. 22).
HBeAg is not needed to decide on treatment (NVHCP p. 22).

clinicalManagement.title: Start antiviral
actions: Tenofovir or entecavir; both have a high barrier to resistance (NVHCP p. 23).
Refer to a Model Treatment Centre for TAF, interferon, decompensation, chemotherapy, virological failure or flares (NVHCP p. 24).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor
actions: ALT and APRI/FIB-4 every 6 months; HBV DNA yearly (NVHCP p. 24).
Renal function on TDF every 3 months in year 1, then 6-monthly (NVHCP p. 47).

clinicalManagement.title: Pregnancy and newborn
actions: Assess the mother for treatment; caesarean only for obstetric reasons (NVHCP p. 24).
Baby: hepatitis B vaccine birth dose within 24 hours plus doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; hepatitis B immunoglobulin 0.5 mL (100 IU) within 12–24 hours in the other thigh (NVHCP pp. 25, 27).

medicationPlan.note: All doses from NVHCP Technical Guidelines for Hepatitis B (2019): TDF 300 mg, entecavir 0.5 mg (1 mg if decompensated), TAF 25 mg once daily; paediatric entecavir by weight. The fixed-dose antiretroviral tablet composition follows the national ART programme; confirm with the National AIDS Control Organisation formulary. Hepatitis B vaccine is given to the baby within 24 hours plus 3 further doses. Not clinically reviewed.

teaching.scope: Chronic hepatitis B in primary and specialist care.
learningObjectives: Stage liver disease with APRI, FIB-4 and ultrasound.
keyPoints: Cirrhosis: treat regardless of DNA or ALT.
Tenofovir or entecavir; never lamivudine alone.
Women who may become pregnant: tenofovir.
Birth-dose vaccine within 24 hours for every baby of an HBsAg-positive mother.
pitfalls: Stopping antivirals and triggering a flare.
Using entecavir in a woman planning pregnancy.
Missing HIV co-infection before starting therapy.

patientEducation: Hepatitis B is long-term; take tablets every day and do not stop without advice.
Family members and partners should be tested and vaccinated.
Breastfeeding is safe if the baby is vaccinated (NVHCP p. 25).
lifestyleAndDiet: Safe sex and no sharing of needles, razors or toothbrushes.
